# lj

A file manager and a terminal for a machine you cannot reach.

One side holds a port, the other dials out to it. No inbound port is needed
on the machine that cannot be reached. Open the page in a browser and you
can browse that machine's files, edit them, move them around, and run
commands on it -- with the colour they were printed in.

```
repo/
  pyproject.toml            <- packaging metadata; the package sits one level
  lj/                          below it, or the install silently fails
    __init__.py
    listen.py                 lj listen      the side that holds the port
    agent.py                     the file and command operations
    wire.py                      the command/result protocol
    page.py                      the browser UI
    dialer.py                 lj dialer      the far side
    selftest.py               python -m lj.selftest
    gui.py                    lj gui         the window

machine A  (no inbound port)            machine B  (holds the port)
  lj dialer  --POST /res-------------->  lj listen  :10000
      ^                                    ^
      |                           GET /cmd |  the far side collects work
      +---- GET /cmd ------------- POST /cmd   the browser asks for something
                                          ^
                                          |
                                        browser
```

Standard library only. No dependencies, no install step.

## Use

**On the machine with the browser** - it holds the port:

```bash
lj listen
```

```
  lj listen  (light_jupyter 5.0.0)
    listening : 0.0.0.0:10000
    reachable : <this machine's address>:10000
    token     : lj_FE3FQK8Z...           (loaded from ~/.lj/token)

  browser : http://<this machine's address>:10000/#token=lj_FE3FQK8Z...

  hand this to the far side:

    lj dialer <this machine's address>:10000/#token=lj_FE3FQK8Z...

  ctrl-c to stop
```

The address is this machine's own, read at run time -- the first IPv4
that is not loopback. It is not written down anywhere: the same
machine changes address when it changes network.

Copy the `browser :` line as it stands - the token is in the fragment, so
the page authenticates itself. The fragment is never sent to the server,
so the token cannot leak into a log or a `Referer` header.

The address in that line is the machine's own IPv4, read at run time -
the first one that is not loopback. Not `127.0.0.1`: that works only on
the machine running the listener, and the browser line is the one a
person pastes into a browser that is somewhere else.

**On the machine that cannot be reached** - it dials out:

```bash
lj dialer <this machine's address>:10000/#token=lj_FE3FQK8Z...
```

That is the whole setup. It polls the listener, does what the browser
asks, and brings the answers back. It runs until you stop it.

`lj dialer` IS the worker. There is no `--worker` flag and no other
mode: one command that does one thing.

**The line the listener prints is what you hand over.** It carries the
token, so nothing has to be added to it:

```
    lj dialer <this machine's address>:10000/#token=lj_FE3FQK8Z...
```

The token is in the fragment because that is where the browser's URL
puts it, and a fragment is never sent to the server. The far side reads
it out of the target, so `--token` is not needed:

```bash
lj dialer <this machine's address>:10000/#token=lj_FE3FQK8Z...  # the token comes along
lj dialer --target <this machine's address>:10000 --token lj_...  # the same, spelled out
```

The target may also be given as a positional argument. With no target at
all, both print their usage rather than an error that does not say what
to type.

The far side works inside a root, so a stray path cannot walk the whole
filesystem:

```bash
lj dialer ... --root /srv/project
```

`--root` defaults to the current directory.

| **v4.0.0** | `lj remote` and `lj dialer` are one command: `lj dialer --worker` is the far side's worker, and without it `lj dialer` is the messenger. |
| **v5.0.0** | the messenger is gone. `lj dialer` is the worker -- there is no `--worker` flag, no `-m`, no REPL, and the `/msg`, `/in` and `/send` endpoints are gone too. One command, one job. |

## A window instead of a terminal

`lj gui` opens the listener as a window: a start button, the address to
hand to the far side, and a log. It is a view over the same server --
the HTTP handling and the token are `lj.listen`'s, imported and driven,
not reimplemented. The command line still works and nothing here is
required to use `lj`.

**Closing the window takes the server down with it.** The listener is a
thread in the window's own process, so the port would go when the
process does -- but the window can close while the process lives on, and
a server left running in that gap keeps the port and answers the *next*
launch with the old token. That reads exactly like the new one failing.
So the port is released on the way out: the close button, the end of the
mainloop, and an exception in a callback all stop the server, and the
close waits for the port to be free rather than assuming it.

```bash
lj gui
```

## Endpoints

One path per direction — an endpoint cannot mean both:

| method | path | who | meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `GET` | `/` | anyone | the page |
| `POST` | `/cmd` | page | ask the far side to do something |
| `GET` | `/cmd` | far side | take the work that was asked for |
| `POST` | `/res` | far side | bring the answer back |
| `GET` | `/res` | page | take the answers that came back |

The endpoints that carried messages — `/msg`, `/in` and `/send` — are
gone. They 404, and the self-test asserts that, so they cannot come
back quietly.

Every data endpoint requires the token (`X-LJ-Token` header, or the
`lj_token` cookie for the page).

Each request carries a sequence number, and the answers carry it back, so
the page matches them up itself. That means an answer can come back in a
different order than the requests went out — which happens as soon as two
operations overlap, and which a request/response design has to allow for.

Both queues are bounded (256 commands, 1024 results). A browser that
never collects its results cannot make the listener grow without limit.

## Commands

### `lj gui`

The listener in a window. No flags -- it is the same thing `lj listen`
does, with buttons.

### `lj listen`

| flag | |
|---|---|
| `--port N` | listen port (default `10000`) |
| `--host ADDR` | bind address (default `0.0.0.0` - must be reachable by the sender) |
| `--token-file PATH` | where the token lives (default `~/.lj/token`) |
| `--regen-token` | mint a new token, discarding the old one |
| `--print-only` | print the banner and exit |

### `lj dialer`

The far side. It polls the listener, does what the browser asks, and
brings the answers back. It runs until you stop it.

| flag | |
|---|---|
| `TARGET` | where the listener is; the same thing as `--target` |
| `--target IP[:PORT]` | where the listener is; may carry the token as a fragment |
| `--token TOKEN` | the token; not needed when the target carries it |
| `--root DIR` | the tree the browser may touch (default: the home directory) |
| `--interval SEC` | seconds between polls (default: `1`) |
| `--timeout SEC` | per-request timeout (default: `15`) |
| `--once` | do one poll and exit |
| `--print-only` | print the banner and exit |

## The token

- 256 bits from `secrets`, rendered in a Crockford-style alphabet (no `I`,
  `L`, `O`, `U`, so a token read off a screen cannot be mistyped into a
  different valid token)
- persisted at `~/.lj/token`, mode `0600`
- compared with `hmac.compare_digest`, so a wrong token cannot be
  brute-forced by timing
- sent as the `X-LJ-Token` header; the browser passes it as the `lj_token`
  cookie because a navigation cannot set headers

Regenerate with `lj listen --regen-token`. The old URL stops
working immediately.

## Test

```bash
python -m lj.selftest
```

196 checks: token properties, target parsing, the HTTP surface, that a wrong
token is rejected on every path, that the message endpoints are gone, that
the page can authenticate, that the dialer's CLI handles its failure modes,
and that no byte-stream/terminal surface has crept in (see Scope). The
`0600` assertion only runs where POSIX permission bits mean something
(not on Windows/NTFS).

The suite leaves nothing running: a normal exit reaps every child, and a
run that is killed leaves its pids in a file that the next run cleans up.

## Install

Standard library only, so there is nothing to resolve. Either run it from a
clone:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/LIU-Xnd/light-jupyter.git
cd light-jupyter
lj listen
```

or install it, which puts `lj` on PATH everywhere:

```bash
python -m pip install -e .          # editable: git pull updates the install
lj listen
```

`#egg=` is required on an editable install of a subdirectory URL - pip cannot
infer the project name from `#subdirectory` alone:

```bash
python -m pip install -e "git+https://github.com/LIU-Xnd/light-jupyter.git#subdirectory=lj&egg=lj"
```

If `github.com:443` is blocked on your network, `git clone
git@github.com:LIU-Xnd/light-jupyter.git` works the same.

### As an MSI

There is also an installer, with the window and a Start Menu shortcut:

```bash
python tools/build_msi.py  # -> appdist/windows/dist/lj-<version>.msi
```

It bundles a Python runtime, so it installs on a machine with nothing on
it -- no Python, no pip, no conda. The build needs
[WiX](https://wixtoolset.org) (v6 or later) and `pyappdist`; point
`PYAPPDIST_WIN_WIX` at `wix.exe` if it is not on PATH.

The installer is a normal wizard: a licence page, a **Destination
Folder** page where you can change the folder or browse for one, a
progress bar, and a page that says it is done.

The MSI is unsigned, so Windows will warn about an unknown publisher. That
is the price of not having a signing certificate.

### As a Linux binary

The far side can also be frozen into one file, so it runs on a machine
with nothing installed -- no Python, no conda, no pip:

```bash
python tools/build_linux_binary.py   # -> dist/linux/lj
```

```bash
./lj dialer <ip>:<port>/#token=<token> --root ~/project
```

The dialer is the half that matters: it is the one that runs on the box
that cannot be reached, and it is the one that has to carry its own
interpreter.

It has to be built on Linux, and on the machine it will run on or an
older one: the binary links against the glibc of the system that built
it, and glibc only goes forwards. Built on Ubuntu 20.04 it needs
GLIBC_2.14, so it runs on 20.04 and everything newer.

## Security

- 256-bit token compared in constant time, stored `0600`
- a wrong token is rejected on every path (`POST /cmd`, `GET /cmd`,
  `POST /res`, `GET /res`)
- the page itself is unauthenticated (a static shell); all data requires
  the token
- the far side's operations are confined to `--root`: a path that escapes
  it is refused

**The token is a shell credential now.** Holding it lets someone read,
write and delete files on the far side and run commands there, with that
account's rights. It was a messaging credential before; it is a password
for that machine now. The traffic is plain HTTP, so use a network you
control, and give the far side an account you would be willing to lose.

## Scope: a file manager and a command runner

The far side can be asked to list a directory, read a file, write one,
move it, copy it, delete it, and to run a command and return its output.

**What it is not:** there is no PTY and no byte stream. A command runs to
completion and its output comes back whole. There is no interactive
session, no window size, no signal channel and no job control.

That is deliberate. A real interactive terminal needs a PTY, a resize
channel, a signal channel and flow control — and a browser that emulates
one properly is xterm.js, which is a large dependency to carry for a tool
whose point is being small. Every operation here is a request that comes
back whole, so a timeout costs one operation rather than a session that
has to be detected and rebuilt.

What you get instead is what a person actually wants from a box they
cannot reach: run something, see what it printed, in colour.

The command line is split into arguments the way a shell would split it
(quotes and backslash escapes honoured), but it is **not** handed to a
shell: no expansion, no globbing, no pipes, no redirection. The process
is run directly, which is why a command cannot be tricked into running
something else.

`lj/selftest.py` asserts the boundary that is left: it fails if a
`/raw`, `/stream` or `/ws` endpoint appears, or if a PTY is opened
anywhere in the agent.

## Limitations

- one shared token, so anything holding it can drive the far side
- the terminal is not interactive: no prompt, no pipes, no redirection, no
  Ctrl-C, and a command that waits for input will sit until the timeout
- a file is edited as text; binary files can be listed, copied and
  deleted, but not opened in the editor
- "upload" and "download" are copy and read -- the files are on the far
  side, so the browser's own disk is not a source or a destination
- the port on the listening machine must be reachable by the far side
